About this map

Version 0.26.0. What it is, and where everything came from

A fan-made, non-commercial star map of the Project Daybreak universe, laid over the real Milky Way. Real stars are where the catalogues put them. Daybreak locations are placed from the Daybreak charts and wiki where they give a position and constructed where they do not; the info panel says which is which for every object.

Halo © Microsoft Corporation. This map was created under Microsoft's "Game Content Usage Rules" using assets from Halo, and it is not endorsed by or affiliated with Microsoft. Game Content Usage Rules

Built by Faber and Tacitus. Faber built the map: the code, the placements, the system models and the write-ups. Tacitus made the Project Daybreak charts and the Daybreak galaxy map that the placements follow.

Lore

Project Daybreak Wikidaybreak.miraheze.org, released under CC BY-SA 4.0. Where an object has a wiki article, its opening lines are the overview, quoted, attributed and linked in the panel.

Daybreak chartsPositions in human and Covenant space follow the three Daybreak charts: the Human Sphere chart (2565), the ONI Project LEVIATHAN Spinward strategic map (2576), the Siakar Expanse chart and the Covenant Sphere heatmap (1,000 ly grid), with the Halo Array placed as on the Daybreak galaxy map ("The Milky Way / Project LEVIATHAN", Tacitus, 2021). Where a chart and a wiki page disagree, the map follows the chart.

Star and deep sky data

Augmented Tycho-HYG (AT-HYG) v4.0By David Nash (astronexus), codeberg.org/astronexus/athyg, CC BY-SA 4.0. 354,212 of the 634,031 stars in the field, the named-star list and the HIP, HD, HR, Gliese, Bayer, Flamsteed, Tycho-2 and Gaia DR3 designations come from it. AT-HYG is itself compiled from Hipparcos and Tycho-2 (ESA), Gaia DR3, the Henry Draper catalogue, the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, the Gliese-Jahreiss catalogue and the IAU star names. The Hipparcos distance switch in Settings uses the HYG parallaxes carried in the same catalogue.

Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars (GCNS)Gaia Collaboration, Smart, R. L., et al. 2021, A&A, 649, A6, "Gaia Early Data Release 3: The Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars", via the CDS VizieR catalogue J/A+A/649/A6. The 279,819 faint stars and brown dwarfs within 100 pc that AT-HYG does not carry, with their Gaia EDR3, 2MASS and CATWISE names, come from it. The 863 brown dwarfs (767 typed by SIMBAD, 96 candidates by colour and absolute magnitude) are drawn and typed as such.

SIMBADThis research has made use of the SIMBAD database, operated at CDS, Strasbourg, France (Wenger, M., et al. 2000, A&AS, 143, 9). Every other identifier a star carries, its object type, and the adopted parallax that places each star within 100 pc come from a SIMBAD extract taken on 23 September 2026.

2MASS and CATWISENames from the Two Micron All Sky Survey (Skrutskie, M. F., et al. 2006, AJ, 131, 1163) and CATWISE2020 (Marocco, F., et al. 2021, ApJS, 253, 8), as carried by GCNS.

GaiaThis work has made use of data from the European Space Agency (ESA) mission Gaia, processed by the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC). Funding for the DPAC has been provided by national institutions, in particular the institutions participating in the Gaia Multilateral Agreement.

Globular clustersHarris, W. E. 1996, AJ, 112, 1487 (2010 edition), mwgc.dat.

Supernova remnantsGreen, D. A. 2024, "A Catalogue of Galactic Supernova Remnants (2024 October version)", Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge; Green, D. A. 2025, Journal of Astrophysics and Astronomy, 46, 14. Distances from the papers named in each remnant's panel.

Local Group galaxiesMcConnachie, A. W. 2012, AJ, 144, 4, "The Observed Properties of Dwarf Galaxies in and around the Local Group", with later discoveries from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Nebulae, molecular clouds and open clustersPositions and distances from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and the papers named in each object's panel, with Gaia distances where they exist.

Constellation figuresStellarium "modern" sky culture, CC BY-SA 4.0, drawn between the Hipparcos stars at their real 3D positions.

Galactic plane gridLongitude spokes and distance rings after the NASA/JPL-Caltech (R. Hurt) annotated Milky Way diagram; the grid is computed, not traced.

SolPlanetary positions from the JPL approximate Keplerian elements (Standish, J2000 ± 2 centuries).

Star display namesCross-checked during the build against taiyin-star-catalog-lite by RedSC1 (MPL-2.0). No code from it ships with this map.

Art and design

Planet texturesSolar System Scope textures, CC BY 4.0: Mercury, Venus, Earth (day, night and specular), the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and its rings, Uranus and Neptune.

Moon and dwarf-planet texturesIo, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Enceladus and Pluto from NASA 3D Resources (NASA/JPL-Caltech), free and without copyright under NASA's media usage guidelines.

HologramsAny body without a public texture, and every constructed system, is drawn as a hologram placeholder.

Galaxy, nebula and cluster renderingProcedural, made for this project. The Halo rings are drawn as procedural models.

Software

three.js r170 (MIT licence). Fonts: Inter (Rasmus Andersson), Chakra Petch (Cadson Demak) and IBM Plex Mono (IBM), all under the SIL Open Font Licence, bundled with the app. Desktop build: Tauri (MIT / Apache-2.0). Source and releases: github.com/Installation04/Daybreak-StarMap. The map's own code is MIT; the Daybreak placement data is CC BY-SA 4.0.

Found an error?

Distances and positions in fiction are often contradictory. If you have a source that beats the one this map used, the panel names what it used, and the GitHub page takes reports.

How to use this map

How to use this map

Everything you need, in about five minutes

What you're looking at

The Milky Way from outside, about 100,000 light years corner to corner, with Project Daybreak laid over the top of it.

One unit here is one light year. The bright smear in the middle is the galactic core. Sol is the small yellow dot 26,000 light years out on a spiral arm.

Two spheres sit on that galaxy. The Human Sphere is 484 systems from the 2565 chart and Daybreak's own Human Sphere page, each one placed on the real star it names where a catalogue star can be tied to it. The Covenant Sphere is 690 systems read off the Covenant worlds table, the two strategic charts and the Covenant Sphere heatmap. Everything else on screen came out of the star catalogues: 634,031 stars in the field, 9,843 of them named, and every one of them can be clicked, plus the nebulae, the clusters and the small galaxies orbiting ours.

Moving around

Left mouse drags the view round. Scroll moves you in and out, and it zooms towards your cursor rather than the middle of the screen, so point at what you want before you scroll.

Click something to select it. You get a ring round it, its name in the top right, and a panel of everything the map knows about it. That includes the anonymous dots of the star field: click one and the panel names it by its best designation and lists every catalogue identifier it carries, from HIP and HD down to Gaia, 2MASS and the survey names. Settings has a switch if you would rather clicks only landed on named things.

Selecting doesn't move you anywhere. It hands the camera something to pivot around, so you can circle a thing without drifting off it. When you want to go there, click it again, or press Fly to.

There are plus and minus buttons in the bottom right if your trackpad is being difficult.

Finding things

The search box at the top reaches everything on the map, and that now includes the catalogue. Type a Daybreak system name, a world, a sector, a domain, or a designation: HD 128620, hd128620, HR 5459, GJ 559, TYC 9007-5849-1 and a bare Gaia source id all resolve, and from three characters on the search also reaches the whole star field, so a 2MASS name or a Wolf, Ross or LP number finds its star. Names rank above designations, so searching Soell gets you Soell rather than a star that happens to carry the number.

It selects rather than flies. Planets and moons break that rule, because from outside its own system a planet has no size at all and selecting one would show you nothing, so those take you in.

The panel down the left is the same catalogue sorted into categories. Use it when you want to go somewhere but don't know what it's called. It also holds three lists that are hard to reach any other way: systems with named worlds, the 15 systems Daybreak lists with no real star behind them, and the 70 places where Daybreak and the star catalogues disagree.

The two spheres, and the filters

The filter panel opens on the left, next to Browse. Two tabs, because the spheres are organised differently.

Human Sphere is a quadrant to sector tree, 5 quadrants and 113 sectors, exactly as the Human Sphere page nests them. Distance band from Sol is a separate axis rather than a branch of that tree, because Gaia moves a few systems into a band their listed sector does not sit in. Covenant Sphere is quartal to domain to location, 4 quartals, 106 domains, 237 locations.

Every node carries its count. There is a box to narrow the list by typing, All, None and Invert buttons, and an "only" control that appears when you hover a node.

Filtered-out systems drop out of the star cloud, lose their labels and stop being clickable. By default they stay as faint dots at about a fifth brightness, so you can still see the shape of what you have hidden. Turn that off and they go completely.

Two things deliberately ignore the filter. Slipspace routes stay drawn, with a small dot left on any vertex whose system is hidden so no line ends in empty space. The Browse panel stays complete, and selecting a hidden system from search brings that one system back until you select something else. The filter can hide a thing. It can never make it unreachable.

One oddity worth knowing: 36 systems belong to both spheres. Twenty sit on a real star that Daybreak gives a human designation. The other sixteen are Covenant-held systems that the Human Sphere page nonetheless lists under a human sector, from Verso 792 out to Kayra 102; they are drawn at their chart position but they now count into the human tree as well. A system in both trees is drawn if either filter admits it, so picking a single human quadrant will usually return a few more systems than that quadrant's own count, because the Covenant tab is still letting the dual-listed ones through.

Slipspace routes

The Arterial Network page gives the crossing routes. The Human Sphere chart of 2565 gives 77 more, with the jump length printed on most legs, and those lengths are in the route panel. The Spinward strategic map of 2576 and the Siakar Expanse chart give the Covenant side.

Where the chart and the wiki disagree about where a route goes, the chart wins. The three charts, the Human Sphere of 2565, the Spinward strategic map of 2576 and the Siakar Expanse, are the source for both spheres.

Routes that leave the charts get a 45 light year stub in the right direction and a note saying where they were heading.

Going into a star system

Get within about a third of a light year of a star and the map stops treating it as a point of light and builds the system around it, with planets, moons and orbit lines.

Try Sol. Select it, press Enter system, and note that you land on Earth rather than the Sun.

Everything in here is true scale against true orbital distance, which is unflattering to planets. They are specks until you are almost on top of them. Positions run on the real clock, so Jupiter is wherever Jupiter is this afternoon. The house icon at the top gets you back to the galaxy.

The Array

Seven installations, placed from Daybreak's own galaxy map.

Installation 04 sits on Soell and has a full system around it. The ring is drawn broken, with its debris field on the line between Threshold and Basis, because Daybreak has it destroyed on 22 September 2552 and the field under joint quarantine. Installation 05 sits where the galaxy map puts it, 8,984 light years out, with the Coelest system built around it from the worlds table. Installation 02 gets the Galar system, because Daybreak names both the system and the anchor.

The other four are ellipses. Daybreak names no system for them, so I have drawn the region and stopped there rather than inventing a star.

Every ring in Daybreak sits between a giant planet and one of its moons. Where the wiki names the anchor, that is the anchor. Where it doesn't, the panel says the placement is constructed and tells you what it was constructed from. The dashed shapes with no ring inside them are the hatched areas off the same galaxy map: possible, unconfirmed, and labelled as such.

Reading the panel

Top of the panel is a passage from the Daybreak wiki and a link to the article. Then the figures. Anything the map constructed rather than took from Daybreak is flagged in that table, and the basis is named: the catalogue star, the 2565 chart, the 2576 chart, the heatmap fit, or by hand.

Stars carry their full set of designations at the foot of the panel. Systems on the 2565 chart carry their population class and their worlds with the status the chart gives them, which is where the glassed colonies show up.

Below that are the notes on where the placement came from.

Where this map is guessing

More than I would like, and it tells you every time.

The Covenant charts carry no elevation at all, so every Covenant height on this map is invented. Until d10 each system drew its own at random, which is why the Siakar Expanse used to stand up like a hedge: 197 systems inside a box 200 light years across, each at its own unrelated height.

Height now comes from a smooth field sampled at the system's chart position, so neighbours sit at similar heights and the ground rises and falls instead of jumping. Two sliders in settings drive it. The cap sets how far off the plane the field can reach, and the terrain scale sets how quickly it changes. Under them is a line telling you what the current settings actually do to systems 75 to 100 light years apart. None of this is canon. It is a plausible shape standing in for elevation data that does not exist yet.

Urs comes out 3,870 light years from Sol on the 2576 chart's own scale bar against the wiki's 3,500. The map uses the chart. Fifteen systems have no real star behind them at all.

None of it is hidden. It is all in the panels.

Settings

Gear icon, top right.

Every layer has a switch. Turning things off is the fastest fix for a view that has become unreadable, and it is almost always the constellations or the labels doing it.

Two things in here are worth finding on purpose. Marker distances switches the whole map between Gaia DR3 and Hipparcos, which moves several hundred stars and is the quickest way to see how much the catalogues argue. Sector plane draws Daybreak's own geometry through Sol, with the 30 degree sector spokes and drop lines to the plane, and it makes the sector assignments legible in a way no amount of rotating does.

Galaxy volume is the setting that costs real money in frame rate. Auto benchmarks your machine on load and usually picks right.

If it runs badly

The galaxy is a genuine volume being raymarched, not a photo on a plane, and that is where your frames are going.

Set Galaxy volume to Low. That alone fixes most of it. Still bad? Render scale down to 0.75. After that you are into turning layers off, and nebulae and clusters is the expensive one. There is a Copy diagnostics button under the performance overlay if you want to send me the numbers.

You need WebGL2, which every browser has had since 2021. Beyond that this wants a desktop graphics card. It will technically run on a laptop.

Something looks wrong

Probably, yes.

Daybreak's distances come from several places that were never reconciled, and the star catalogues have moved under all of them since. Where Daybreak and a catalogue disagree about which star a system is, Daybreak wins and the override is flagged. Where a chart and the wiki disagree, both are recorded.

Every panel names its source. If you have a better one, tell me.
